claim: Elevated levels of IFNγ in SLE patients correlate with expansion of the T-bet expressing IgDnegCD27negCD11c+CXCR5neg (DN2) pre-antibody secreting cell (pre-ASC) subset.
source: We show that elevated levels of IFNγ in SLE patients correlate with expansion of the T-bet expressing IgDnegCD27negCD11c+CXCR5neg (DN2) pre-antibody secreting cell (pre-ASC) subset.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis between plasma IFNγ levels and frequency of T-bethi DN2 cells in SLE patients, as shown in Figure 1h-i.

claim: Naïve B cells form T-bethi pre-ASCs following stimulation with Th1 cells or with IFNγ, IL-2, anti-Ig and TLR7/8 ligand.
source: We demonstrate that naïve B cells form T-bethi pre-ASCs following stimulation with either Th1 cells or with IFNγ, IL-2, anti-Ig and TLR7/8 ligand
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro culture experiments showing T-bet expression and pre-ASC phenotype in naïve B cells stimulated with these conditions, as shown in Figures 2-4.

claim: IL-21 dependent ASC formation is significantly enhanced by IFNγ or IFNγ-producing T cells.
source: and that IL-21 dependent ASC formation is significantly enhanced by IFNγ or IFNγ-producing T cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing increased ASC frequencies in cultures containing IFNγ or Th1 cells compared to controls, as shown in Figures 2, 4, and 5.

claim: IFNγ promotes ASC development by synergizing with IL-2 and TLR7/8 ligands to induce genome-wide epigenetic reprogramming of B cells.
source: IFNγ promotes ASC development by synergizing with IL-2 and TLR7/8 ligands to induce genome-wide epigenetic reprogramming of B cells
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data showing differential chromatin accessibility patterns in B cells stimulated with IFNγ, IL-2, and R848, as shown in Figure 7.

claim: IFNγ-induced epigenetic reprogramming results in increased chromatin accessibility surrounding IRF4 and BLIMP1 binding motifs.
source: which results in increased chromatin accessibility surrounding IRF4 and BLIMP1 binding motifs
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq analysis showing enriched accessibility at IRF4 and BLIMP1 binding motifs in IFNγ-stimulated cells, as shown in Figure 7h-i.

claim: IFNγ induces epigenetic remodeling of IL21R and PRDM1 loci.
source: and epigenetic remodeling of IL21R and PRDM1 loci.
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data showing differentially accessible regions (DARs) at the IL21R and PRDM1 loci in IFNγ-stimulated cells, as shown in Figure 7j-k.

claim: IFNγ signals poise B cells to differentiate by increasing their responsiveness to IL-21.
source: Finally, we show that IFNγ signals poise B cells to differentiate by increasing their responsiveness to IL-21.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing increased IL-21R expression and enhanced STAT3 phosphorylation in response to IL-21 in IFNγ-primed B cells, as shown in Figure 6j-k and Figure 7l-m.

claim: SLE is characterized by progressive dysregulation of the innate and adaptive arms of the immune system.
source: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) is characterized by progressive dysregulation of the innate and adaptive arms of the immune system, which ultimately leads to loss of immune tolerance in B and T lymphocytes and the production of autoantibodies (Abs) by Ab-secreting B cells (ASCs) (Tsokos et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tsokos et al., 2016.

claim: The hallmark SLE autoAbs recognize nuclear proteins and nucleic acids.
source: The hallmark SLE autoAbs recognize nuclear proteins and nucleic acids (Gatto et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gatto et al., 2016.

claim: Nuclear proteins and nucleic acids are ligands for TLR7 and TLR9 that are expressed by innate immune cells and B cells.
source: which are also ligands for TLR7 and TLR9 that are expressed by innate immune cells and B cells (Avalos et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Avalos et al., 2010.

claim: SLE autoAbs bound to their autoAgs form immune complexes, which are responsible for many of the clinical manifestations of SLE, particularly those associated with organ damage.
source: SLE autoAbs bound to their autoAgs form immune complexes, which are responsible for many of the clinical manifestations of SLE, particularly those associated with organ damage (Gatto et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gatto et al., 2016.

claim: Belimumab is the only new drug approved to treat SLE in decades and targets B cells.
source: Consistent with the important role for B cells and ASCs in SLE pathogenesis (Sanz, 2014), the only new drug approved to treat SLE in decades, Belimumab, targets B cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sanz, 2014 and general knowledge about Belimumab approval.

claim: SLE patient PBMCs often exhibit a type I interferon (IFN) transcriptional signature.
source: SLE patient PBMCs often exhibit a type I interferon (IFN) transcriptional signature and systemic IFNα is elevated in many patients (Obermoser and Pascual, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Obermoser and Pascual, 2010.

claim: Systemic IFNα is elevated in many SLE patients.
source: SLE patient PBMCs often exhibit a type I interferon (IFN) transcriptional signature and systemic IFNα is elevated in many patients (Obermoser and Pascual, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Obermoser and Pascual, 2010.

claim: IFNγ is increased in some SLE patients.
source: It is less well appreciated that IFNγ is also increased in some SLE patients (Csiszár et al., 2000; Harigai et al., 2008; Pollard et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Csiszár et al., 2000; Harigai et al., 2008; Pollard et al., 2013.

claim: A distinct IFNγ transcription signature can be detected in PBMCs from a portion of SLE patients.
source: and that a distinct IFNγ transcription signature can be detected in PBMCs from a portion of SLE patients (Chiche et al., 2014; Welcher et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chiche et al., 2014; Welcher et al., 2015.

claim: Elevated serum IFNγ can be observed years before IFNα or autoAbs are detected in SLE patients.
source: Interestingly, elevated serum IFNγ can be observed years before IFNα or autoAbs are detected in SLE patients and much earlier than clinical disease (Munroe et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Munroe et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2016.

claim: CXCR3 and T-bet are more highly expressed by circulating B cells from SLE patients compared to healthy controls.
source: For example, two IFNγ-inducible proteins, CXCR3 and T-bet, are more highly expressed by circulating B cells from SLE patients compared to healthy controls (Harigai et al., 2008; Nicholas et al., 2008; Lit et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2018; Jenks et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Harigai et al., 2008; Nicholas et al., 2008; Lit et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2018; Jenks et al., 2018.

claim: Clinical disease in mouse SLE models is dependent on B cell-specific expression of the IFNγR.
source: Moreover, data from mouse SLE models show that clinical disease is dependent on B cell-specific expression of the IFNγR and the IFNγ- induced transcription factors (TF) STAT1 (Domeier et al., 2016; Jackson et al., 2016; Thibault et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Domeier et al., 2016; Jackson et al., 2016; Thibault et al., 2008.

claim: Clinical disease in some mouse SLE models is dependent on B cell-specific expression of T-bet.
source: and T-bet in some (Rubtsova et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2017) but not all (Jackson et al., 2016; Du et al., 2019) models.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rubtsova et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2017; Jackson et al., 2016; Du et al., 2019.

claim: CD11chi B cells are also called age associated B cells (ABCs).
source: Two interrelated populations of circulating B cells present in SLE patients, namely the CD11chi B cells, which are also called age associated B cells (ABCs) (Karnell et al., 2017; Rubtsov et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Karnell et al., 2017; Rubtsov et al., 2017.

claim: IgDnegCD27neg B double negative (BDN) B cells are often referred to as 'atypical' memory B cells.
source: and the IgDnegCD27neg B double negative (BDN) B cells, which are often referred to as 'atypical' memory B cells (Wei et al., 2007; Portugal et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wei et al., 2007; Portugal et al., 2017.

claim: CD11chi B cells and BDN cells are reported to express the IFNγ-inducible TF T-bet.
source: are reported to express the IFNγ-inducible TF T-bet.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the context and prior citations in the paragraph.

claim: CD11chi B cells and BDN cells are present in low numbers in the blood or tonsils of healthy individuals.
source: These B cells, which may have been exposed to IFNγ at some step in their developmental process, are present in low numbers in the blood or tonsils of healthy individuals (Ehrhardt et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ehrhardt et al., 2005.

claim: CD11chi B cells and BDN cells are reported to be expanded in chronically infected, aging and autoimmune individuals.
source: and are reported to be expanded in chronically infected, aging and autoimmune individuals (reviewed in Naradikian et al., 2016), including patients with SLE (Wang et al., 2018; Jenks et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Naradikian et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2018; Jenks et al., 2018.

claim: The CD11chi population found in SLE patients is heterogeneous and contains CD11c-expressing IgDnegCD27+ switched memory (BSW) cells, IgDnegCD27neg naïve (BN) cells and BDN cells.
source: The CD11chi population found in SLE patients is heterogeneous and contains CD11c-expressing IgDnegCD27+ switched memory (BSW) cells, IgDnegCD27neg naïve (BN) cells and BDN cells (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2018.

claim: The BDN population can be subdivided using CD11c and CXCR5 into the DN2 (CD11chiCXCR5neg) subset, which express T-bet, and the DN1 (CD11cloCXCR5+) subset, which does not express T-bet.
source: The BDN population is also heterogeneous and can be subdivided using CD11c and CXCR5 into the DN2 (CD11chiCXCR5neg) subset, which express T-bet, and the DN1 (CD11cloCXCR5+) subset, which does not express T-bet (Jenks et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jenks et al., 2018.

claim: Initial studies examining BDN cells from malaria or HIV-infected individuals described these B cells as anergic.
source: Although initial studies examining BDN cells from malaria or HIV-infected individuals described these B cells as anergic (reviewed in Portugal et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Portugal et al., 2017.

claim: CD11c-expressing IgDnegCD27+CD21lo activated BSW cells from influenza vaccinated humans possess phenotypic and molecular characteristics of pre-ASCs.
source: more recent studies reported that the CD11c-expressing IgDnegCD27+CD21lo activated BSW cells from influenza vaccinated humans (Lau et al., 2017) and HIV infected patients (Knox et al., 2017), as well as the CD11chi cells from SLE patients (Wang et al., 2018) and the CD11chi DN2 cells from SLE patients (Jenks et al., 2018) possess phenotypic and molecular characteristics of pre-ASCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lau et al., 2017.

claim: CD11c-expressing IgDnegCD27+CD21lo activated BSW cells from HIV infected patients possess phenotypic and molecular characteristics of pre-ASCs.
source: more recent studies reported that the CD11c-expressing IgDnegCD27+CD21lo activated BSW cells from influenza vaccinated humans (Lau et al., 2017) and HIV infected patients (Knox et al., 2017), as well as the CD11chi cells from SLE patients (Wang et al., 2018) and the CD11chi DN2 cells from SLE patients (Jenks et al., 2018) possess phenotypic and molecular characteristics of pre-ASCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Knox et al., 2017.

claim: CD11chi cells from SLE patients possess phenotypic and molecular characteristics of pre-ASCs.
source: more recent studies reported that the CD11c-expressing IgDnegCD27+CD21lo activated BSW cells from influenza vaccinated humans (Lau et al., 2017) and HIV infected patients (Knox et al., 2017), as well as the CD11chi cells from SLE patients (Wang et al., 2018) and the CD11chi DN2 cells from SLE patients (Jenks et al., 2018) possess phenotypic and molecular characteristics of pre-ASCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2018.

claim: CD11chi DN2 cells from SLE patients possess phenotypic and molecular characteristics of pre-ASCs.
source: more recent studies reported that the CD11c-expressing IgDnegCD27+CD21lo activated BSW cells from influenza vaccinated humans (Lau et al., 2017) and HIV infected patients (Knox et al., 2017), as well as the CD11chi cells from SLE patients (Wang et al., 2018) and the CD11chi DN2 cells from SLE patients (Jenks et al., 2018) possess phenotypic and molecular characteristics of pre-ASCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jenks et al., 2018.

claim: CD11chi B cells from SLE patients differentiate into ASCs following stimulation.
source: Both the CD11chi B cells and the more narrowly defined DN2 subset from SLE patients differentiate into ASCs following stimulation (Wang et al., 2018; Jenks et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2018; Jenks et al., 2018.

claim: The T-bethi DN2 subset from SLE patients can produce autoAbs.
source: Moreover, the T-bethi DN2 subset from SLE patients can produce autoAbs (Jenks et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jenks et al., 2018.

claim: T-bethi DN2 pre-ASCs correlate with disease severity in SLE patients.
source: Since T-bethi DN2 pre-ASCs produce autoAbs and correlate with disease severity in SLE patients (Jenks et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jenks et al., 2018.

claim: A subset of SLE patients presented with an expanded population of circulating IgDnegCD27neg (double negative, BDN cells).
source: Consistent with our prior studies using a different cohort of SLE patients (Jenks et al., 2018), we observed that a subset of our SLE patients presented with an expanded population of circulating IgDnegCD27neg (double negative, BDN cells) (Figure 1a–b)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1a-b and citation to Jenks et al., 2018.

claim: BDN cells can be subdivided into CD11c+CXCR5neg DN2 cells and CD11cnegCXCR5+ DN1 cells.
source: that could be subdivided into CD11c+CXCR5neg DN2 cells and CD11cnegCXCR5+ DN1 cells (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: DN2 cells, but not DN1 cells, uniformly expressed high levels of T-bet.
source: The DN2 cells, but not the DN1 cells, uniformly expressed high levels of T-bet (Figure 1d)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: T-bethi BDN cells expressed intermediate levels of the ASC-promoting TFs, Blimp1 and IRF4.
source: In agreement with our prior studies, the T-bethi BDN cells (gated as in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b) expressed intermediate levels of the ASC-promoting TFs, Blimp1 and IRF4 (Figure 1e–f,)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1e-f.

claim: The presence of T-bethi BDN cells correlated with anti-Smith autoAb titers in SLE patients.
source: and their presence correlated with anti-Smith autoAb titers in the patients (Figure 1g).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1g.

claim: There is a significant positive correlation between IFNγ and the frequency of T-bethi DN2 cells in SLE patients.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, we observed a significant positive correlation between IFNγ, as well as the IFNγ-induced cytokines CXCL10, IL-6 and TNFα, and the frequency of T-bethi DN2 cells in these individuals (Figure 1h).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1h.

claim: There is a significant positive correlation between CXCL10 and the frequency of T-bethi DN2 cells in SLE patients.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, we observed a significant positive correlation between IFNγ, as well as the IFNγ-induced cytokines CXCL10, IL-6 and TNFα, and the frequency of T-bethi DN2 cells in these individuals (Figure 1h).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1h.

claim: There is a significant positive correlation between IL-6 and the frequency of T-bethi DN2 cells in SLE patients.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, we observed a significant positive correlation between IFNγ, as well as the IFNγ-induced cytokines CXCL10, IL-6 and TNFα, and the frequency of T-bethi DN2 cells in these individuals (Figure 1h).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1h.

claim: There is a significant positive correlation between TNFα and the frequency of T-bethi DN2 cells in SLE patients.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, we observed a significant positive correlation between IFNγ, as well as the IFNγ-induced cytokines CXCL10, IL-6 and TNFα, and the frequency of T-bethi DN2 cells in these individuals (Figure 1h).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1h.

claim: Approximately 50% of HD B cells activated in the presence of IFNγ-producing Th1 cells (Be1 cells) expressed T-bet.
source: After 6 days in culture, approximately 50% of the HD B cells activated in the presence of IFNγ-producing Th1 cells (Be1 cells) expressed T-bet while very few (<3%) of the HD B cells activated with IL-4 producing Th2 cells (Be2 cells) upregulated T-bet (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Very few (<3%) of HD B cells activated with IL-4 producing Th2 cells (Be2 cells) upregulated T-bet.
source: After 6 days in culture, approximately 50% of the HD B cells activated in the presence of IFNγ-producing Th1 cells (Be1 cells) expressed T-bet while very few (<3%) of the HD B cells activated with IL-4 producing Th2 cells (Be2 cells) upregulated T-bet (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Approximately half of the T-bethi B cells present in the Be1 cultures downregulated IgD and were CD19hiCD27negCD11c+FcRL5+CD23neg.
source: Approximately half of the T-bethi B cells present in the Be1 cultures downregulated IgD and these cells were CD19hiCD27negCD11c+FcRL5+CD23neg (Figure 2c).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: More ASCs were found in Be1 co-cultures compared to Be2 co-cultures across multiple experiments using BN and T effectors from different HD pairs.
source: However, we always found more ASCs in the Be1 co-cultures, even across multiple experiments using BN and T effectors from different HD pairs (Figure 2e).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data across multiple experiments shown in Figure 2e.

claim: ASCs, regardless of isotype, were greatly enriched in the Be1 co-cultures compared to Be2 co-cultures.
source: Again, we found that ASCs, regardless of isotype, were greatly enriched in the Be1 co-cultures (Figure 2f–g).
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing increased IgM and IgG ASCs in Be1 cultures, as shown in Figure 2f-g.

claim: The increase in ASCs in Be1 co-cultures was not due to intrinsic differences in the proliferative rates of the cells in each culture.
source: This increase in ASCs in the Be1 co-cultures was not due to intrinsic differences in the proliferative rates of the cells in each culture but rather that a higher proportion of the Be1 cells at each cell division committed to the ASC lineage (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by proliferation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: A higher proportion of Be1 cells at each cell division committed to the ASC lineage compared to Be2 cells.
source: This increase in ASCs in the Be1 co-cultures was not due to intrinsic differences in the proliferative rates of the cells in each culture but rather that a higher proportion of the Be1 cells at each cell division committed to the ASC lineage (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing increased ASC frequency per division in Be1 cultures, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: 427 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified between the BDN cells from the Be1 and Be2 co-cultures.
source: We identified 427 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between the BDN cells from the Be1 and Be2 co-cultures (Figure 3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Significantly higher levels of TBX21 mRNA were observed in the in vitro induced BDN Be1 cells compared to BDN Be2 cells.
source: Consistent with our data showing that T-bet was selectively upregulated in the B cells from Be1 co-cultures, we observed significantly higher levels of TBX21 mRNA in the in vitro induced BDN Be1 cells compared to BDN Be2 cells (Figure 3c).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The transcriptome of the T-bet expressing BDN Be1 cell subset was highly enriched relative to the BDN Be2 cells for genes that are specifically upregulated in the SLE-derived T-bethi DN2 subset.
source: Consistent with our phenotyping data, the transcriptome of the T-bet expressing BDN Be1 cell subset was highly enriched relative to the BDN Be2 cells for genes that are specifically upregulated in the SLE-derived T-bethi DN2 subset (Figure 3d).
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3d comparing Be1 and Be2 BDN cells to SLE DN2 cells.

claim: The transcriptome of the in vitro-induced BDN Be1 population was significantly enriched in expression of genes that are upregulated in ASCs compared to BN cells.
source: Moreover, the transcriptome of the in vitro-induced BDN Be1 population was significantly enriched in expression of genes that are upregulated in ASCs compared to BN cells (Figure 3e)
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3e.

claim: The transcriptome of the in vitro-induced BDN Be1 population was significantly enriched in expression of genes that are upregulated in ASCs compared to mature B cells.
source: mature B cells (Figure 3f)
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3f.

claim: The transcriptome of the in vitro-induced BDN Be1 population was significantly enriched in expression of genes that are upregulated in ASCs compared to switched memory B cells.
source: and switched memory B cells (Figure 3g).
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3g.

claim: Genes that are direct targets of IRF4 and upregulated in ASCs were significantly enriched in the in vitro generated T-bethi Be1 BDN cells relative to the Be2 BDN cells.
source: In addition, genes that are direct targets of IRF4 and upregulated in ASCs (Shaffer et al., 2008) were significantly enriched in the in vitro generated T-bethi Be1 BDN cells relative to the Be2 BDN cells (Figure 3h).
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3h and citation to Shaffer et al., 2008.

claim: Be1 T-bethi BDN cells expressed intermediate levels of IRF4 when compared to CD38hiCD27+ ASCs and IgD+CD27neg B cells.
source: Consistent with this finding, we observed that the Be1 T-bethi BDN cells had undergone multiple rounds of cell division (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and expressed intermediate levels of IRF4 (Figure 3i–j), when compared to the CD38hiCD27+ ASCs and the IgD+CD27neg B cells present in the Be1 cultures.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3i-j.

claim: Significantly more ASCs were found in cultures containing the sorted T-bet expressing Be1 BDN cells compared to Be2 BDN cells.
source: Although ASCs were detected in the cultures containing either Be1 or Be2 BDN cells, significantly more ASCs were found in cultures containing the sorted T-bet expressing Be1 BDN cells (Figure 3l).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3l.

claim: Predicted upstream regulators of the T-bethi BDN pre-ASC transcriptional network include antigen receptor signaling molecules like Btk.
source: These included antigen receptor signaling molecules, like Btk, cytokines, like IFNα, IFNγ, IL-2 and IL-21, and cytokine-induced TFs, like STAT1 and STAT3 (Figure 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by IPA analysis shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Predicted upstream regulators of the T-bethi BDN pre-ASC transcriptional network include cytokines like IFNα, IFNγ, IL-2 and IL-21.
source: These included antigen receptor signaling molecules, like Btk, cytokines, like IFNα, IFNγ, IL-2 and IL-21, and cytokine-induced TFs, like STAT1 and STAT3 (Figure 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by IPA analysis shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Predicted upstream regulators of the T-bethi BDN pre-ASC transcriptional network include cytokine-induced TFs like STAT1 and STAT3.
source: These included antigen receptor signaling molecules, like Btk, cytokines, like IFNα, IFNγ, IL-2 and IL-21, and cytokine-induced TFs, like STAT1 and STAT3 (Figure 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by IPA analysis shown in Figure 4a.

claim: TLR7 and TLR9 were predicted as upstream regulators of the T-bethi BDN Be1 cells.
source: In addition, both TLR7 and TLR9 were predicted as upstream regulators of the T-bethi BDN Be1 cells (Figure 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by IPA analysis shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Endogenous TLR7 and TLR9 ligands are released by dying cells in vitro.
source: This was unexpected, given that we did not add exogenous TLR ligands to the co-cultures, however, endogenous TLR7 and TLR9 ligands are known to be released by dying cells in vitro (Sindhava et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sindhava et al., 2017.

claim: >95% of BN cells activated with anti-Ig, cytokines (IFNγ, IL-2, IL-21 and BAFF) and R848 were IgDnegCD27neg T-bethiIRF4int.
source: We found that >95% of the BN cells activated with these defined stimuli resembled SLE patient T-bethi DN2 cells (Jenks et al., 2018) as the in vitro activated cells were IgDnegCD27neg T-bethiIRF4int, expressed the DN2 markers, CD11c and FcRL5, and were losing expression of CD21 and CXCR5 (Figure 4c–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4c-d.

claim: When HD BN cells were activated without IFNγ, more than 80% of the cells were T-betneg/lo.
source: By contrast, when the cells were activated without IFNγ, more than 80% of the cells were T-betneg/lo (Figure 4g).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: Cells activated without IFNγ failed to upregulate IRF4.
source: While this wasn't particularly surprising, given that T-bet is IFNγ-inducible (Stone et al., 2019), the cells also failed to upregulate IRF4 (Figure 4g)
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4g and citation to Stone et al., 2019.

claim: IFNγ signals are obligate for the in vitro generation of the T-bethiIRF4int BDN pre-ASC like population.
source: indicating that IFNγ signals are obligate for the in vitro generation of the T-bethiIRF4int BDN pre-ASC like population.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the data showing lack of T-bet and IRF4 expression without IFNγ.

claim: CD38hiCD27+ ASCs did not accumulate in cultures containing all stimuli (anti-Ig, cytokines and R848).
source: Although HD BN cells activated with anti-Ig, cytokines and R848 developed in an IFNγ-dependent fashion into T-bethiIRF4int BDN pre-ASC like cells (Figure 4g), CD38hiCD27+ ASCs did not accumulate in the cultures containing all stimuli (Figure 4h).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4h.

claim: ASCs accumulated in cultures when anti-Ig was present only during the first 3 days of culture.
source: However, when anti-Ig was present only during the first 3 days of culture ASCs accumulated in the cultures (Figure 4j).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4j.

claim: Early but transient BCR signals are important for the development and recovery of ASCs from cytokine and R848 stimulated BN cells.
source: These data therefore argued that early but transient BCR signals were important for the development and recovery of ASCs from cytokine and R848 stimulated BN cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the experimental data showing optimal ASC recovery with transient BCR stimulation.

claim: No ASCs were detected in cultures lacking IL-21.
source: By contrast, and consistent with prior reports showing that ASC development from BN cells requires IL-21 (Ettinger et al., 2008; Tangye, 2015), no ASCs were detected in the cultures lacking IL-21 (Figure 4l).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4l and citations to Ettinger et al., 2008; Tangye, 2015.

claim: ASC recovery in cultures lacking R848 or IFNγ was at background levels.
source: Likewise, ASC recovery in cultures lacking R848 or IFNγ was also at background levels (Figure 4l).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4l.

claim: Formation of the T-bethiIRF4int pre-ASC like population required IFNγ signals.
source: Collectively, the data indicated that formation of the T-bethiIRF4int pre-ASC like population required IFNγ signals while the development and recovery of ASCs were dependent on transient BCR signals, IFNγ, R848 and IL-21.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the experimental data showing IFNγ requirement for pre-ASC formation.

claim: The development and recovery of ASCs were dependent on transient BCR signals, IFNγ, R848 and IL-21.
source: Collectively, the data indicated that formation of the T-bethiIRF4int pre-ASC like population required IFNγ signals while the development and recovery of ASCs were dependent on transient BCR signals, IFNγ, R848 and IL-21.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the experimental data showing requirements for ASC development.

claim: CD38hiCD27+ ASCs were essentially undetected in cultures lacking IFNγ in the first 3 days.
source: Moreover, consistent with our prediction, CD38hiCD27+ ASCs, whether measured as the frequency (Figure 5b) or number (Figure 5c) were essentially undetected in cultures lacking IFNγ in the first 3 days.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5b-c.

claim: BN cells that did not receive an IFNγ signal during the priming phase proliferated less over the 6 day culture period.
source: BN cells that did not receive an IFNγ signal during the priming phase proliferated less over the 6 day culture period (Figure 5d), resulting in minimal cell recovery on day 6 (Figure 5e).
evidence: The claim is supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Addition of IFNγ only during the priming phase was sufficient to induce formation of the T-bethiIRF4int pre-ASC population.
source: By contrast, adding IFNγ only during the priming phase was sufficient to induce formation of the T-bethiIRF4int pre-ASC population (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a)
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Early IFNγ signals were required to drive the development of the T-bethi pre-ASC like subset and the formation and recovery of ASCs in the cultures.
source: Thus, early IFNγ signals were required to drive the development of the T-bethi pre-ASC like subset and the formation and recovery of ASCs in the cultures.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the temporal requirement data showing IFNγ is needed early.

claim: When R848 was only added during the first 3 days, ASCs could not be detected in the cultures.
source: When R848 was only added during the first 3 days, ASCs could not be detected in the cultures, whether measured as the frequency (Figure 5f) or number (Figure 5g) of ASCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5f-g.

claim: R848 played both early and late roles in the development of ASCs, with early TLR7/8 signals appearing to promote B cell survival and late TLR7/8 signals promoting proliferation.
source: These data therefore indicated that R848 played both early and late roles in the development of ASCs, with early TLR7/8 signals appearing to promote B cell survival and late TLR7/8 signals promoting proliferation.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the temporal requirement data for R848.

claim: When IL-21 was only included for the first 3 days of the culture, pre-ASCs formed normally but ASCs could not be detected.
source: When IL-21 was only included for the first 3 days of the culture, pre-ASCs formed normally (Figure 5—figure supplement 1g) but ASCs could not be detected whether measured by frequency (Figure 5j) or number (Figure 5k) of ASCs recovered.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5j-k and Figure 5—figure supplement 1g.

claim: Late IL-21 signals were sufficient to drive ASC formation.
source: Therefore, late IL-21 signals were sufficient to drive ASC formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the temporal requirement data showing IL-21 is needed late.

claim: When high dose R848 was included in the cultures, the cells proliferated regardless of whether IFNγ was included in the cultures for the first 3 days.
source: By contrast, when high dose R848 was included in the cultures, the cells proliferated regardless of whether IFNγ was included in the cultures for the first 3 days (Figure 6b).
evidence: The claim is supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: The frequency of ASCs in cultures activated with low dose TLR ligand in the presence of IFNγ was approximately 10-fold higher than that observed for the cultures that lacked IFNγ.
source: Moreover, we observed that the frequency of ASCs in the cultures that were activated with low dose TLR ligand in the presence of IFNγ was approximately 10-fold higher than that observed for the cultures that lacked IFNγ (Figure 6d).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Exposure of BN cells to IFNγ during the initial priming phase allowed these cells to differentiate even in the face of sub-optimal stimulation with R848.
source: Thus, exposure of BN cells to IFNγ during the initial priming phase allowed these cells to differentiate even in the face of sub-optimal stimulation with R848.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the dose-response data showing IFNγ synergy with low-dose R848.

claim: When B cells were exposed to both IL-2 and IFNγ during the early priming phase, the number of ASCs recovered on day 6 was significantly more than seen in the Be.IFNγ or Be.IL2 cultures.
source: However, when B cells were exposed to both IL-2 and IFNγ during the early priming phase, the number of ASCs recovered on day 6 (Figure 6i) was significantly more than seen in the Be.IFNγ or Be.IL2 cultures.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6i.

claim: Early IFNγ and IL-2 signals cooperate to induce formation and recovery of ASCs.
source: Thus, early IFNγ and IL-2 signals cooperate to induce formation and recovery of ASCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the data showing synergy between IFNγ and IL-2.

claim: Following a 20 min exposure to IL-21, phospho-STAT3 levels were increased significantly in the B cells that were exposed to IFNγ during the priming phase.
source: However, following a 20 min exposure to IL-21, phospho-STAT3 levels were increased significantly in the B cells that were exposed to IFNγ during the priming phase (Figure 6k)
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing phospho-STAT3 levels, as shown in Figure 6k.

claim: Early IFNγ stimulation enhanced IL-21R signaling.
source: indicating that early IFNγ stimulation enhanced IL-21R signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the phospho-STAT3 data.

claim: Early IFNγ signals sensitize human BN cells to respond more robustly to stimuli, like TLR7/8 ligands, IL-2 and IL-21, that promote B cell activation, proliferation and differentiation.
source: Collectively, these data show that early IFNγ signals sensitize human BN cells to respond more robustly to stimuli, like TLR7/8 ligands, IL-2 and IL-21, that promote B cell activation, proliferation and differentiation.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the combined data showing IFNγ synergy with multiple stimuli.

claim: The largest number of chromatin accessible regions was seen in the day 3 Be.γ2 cells.
source: As expected, distinct sets of DAR were found in all 4 groups of activated B cells (Figure 7c), however the largest number of chromatin accessible regions was seen in the day 3 Be.γ2 cells (Figure 7c).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 7c.

claim: The chromatin accessibility pattern in the Be.γ2 cells appeared to reflect cooperation or synergy between the IFNγ and IL-2 signals.
source: Moreover, the chromatin accessibility pattern in the Be.γ2 cells appeared to reflect cooperation or synergy between the IFNγ and IL-2 signals (Figure 7c).
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 7c.

claim: Accessibility around STAT5 binding motifs was enriched in IL-2 exposed B cells.
source: Similarly, accessibility around STAT5 binding motifs was enriched in IL-2 exposed B cells (Figure 7e).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 7e.

claim: The Be.γ2 cells exhibited the greatest enrichment in chromatin accessibility surrounding both T-bet and STAT5 binding sites.
source: However, the Be.γ2 cells exhibited the greatest enrichment in chromatin accessibility surrounding both T-bet and STAT5 binding sites (Figure 7d–e), suggesting that IFNγ and IL-2 cooperate to remodel the epigenome.
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 7d-e.

claim: Binding motifs for NF-κB p65 and REL were most accessible in the Be.γ2 cells compared to all other groups.
source: Consistent with this, binding motifs for NF-κB p65 and REL, TFs activated by anti-Ig and TLR7/8 stimulation (Kaileh and Sen, 2012), were most accessible in the Be.γ2 cells compared to all other groups (Figure 7f–g).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 7f-g and citation to Kaileh and Sen, 2012.

claim: Chromatin accessibility surrounding the HOMER-defined IRF4 and BLIMP1 binding motifs was highly enriched in the Be.γ2 cells.
source: Moreover, chromatin accessibility surrounding the HOMER-defined IRF4 and BLIMP1 binding motifs (Heinz et al., 2010) was also highly enriched in the Be.γ2 cells (Figure 7h–i).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 7h-i and citation to Heinz et al., 2010.

claim: 4 DAR at the PRDM1 locus were each more accessible in the Be.γ2 cells relative to the other cells.
source: Consistent with this finding, when we examined the PRDM1 (BLIMP1) locus, we identified 4 DAR that were each more accessible in the Be.γ2 cells relative to the other cells (Figure 7j).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 7j.

claim: 3 of the 4 PRDM1-associated DAR were also seen in T-bethi DN2 cells purified from SLE patients.
source: Moreover, 3 of the 4 PRDM1-associated DAR were also seen in T-bethi DN2 cells purified from SLE patients (Figure 7j), indicating that these DAR were present in the pre-ASC population found in SLE patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data comparison shown in Figure 7j.

claim: One of the DAR at the IL21R locus contained two putative T-bet binding motifs and was directly aligned with a T-bet ChIP-seq peak from GM12878 cells.
source: One of the DAR contained two putative T-bet binding motifs and was directly aligned with a T-bet ChIP-seq peak from GM12878 cells (ENCODE Project Consortium, 2012) (Figure 7k).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data and alignment with ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 7k, with citation to ENCODE Project Consortium, 2012.

claim: The same DAR at the IL21R locus was identified in the SLE patient T-bethi DN2 cells.
source: Interestingly, we identified the same DAR in the SLE patient T-bethi DN2 cells (Figure 7k), which are reported to be highly responsive to IL-21 (Jenks et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data comparison shown in Figure 7k and citation to Jenks et al., 2018.

claim: By day 6, IL-21R expression levels were 5.5–6-fold higher in the B cells that were cultured in the presence of IFNγ during the first 3 days.
source: By day 6 however, IL-21R expression levels were 5.5–6-fold higher in the B cells that were cultured in the presence of IFNγ during the first 3 days (Figure 7m).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7m.

claim: Early IFNγ signals synergize with BCR, TLR and IL-2 signals to induce global changes in chromatin accessibility.
source: Taken together, the data suggested that early IFNγ signals synergize with BCR, TLR and IL-2 signals to induce global changes in chromatin accessibility and promote increased TF binding at T-bet, NF-κB, STAT5, BLIMP1 and IRF4 binding sites as well as chromatin remodeling at the PRDM1 and IL21R loci.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the combined ATAC-seq data.

claim: SLE patient BN cells acquired phenotypic characteristics of the T-bethi DN2 subset following in vitro activation with R848, IL-2, IFNγ and IL-21.
source: Consistent with our prediction, SLE patient BN cells did acquire phenotypic characteristics of the T-bethi DN2 subset following in vitro activation with R848, IL-2, IFNγ and IL-21 (Figure 8b).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8b.

claim: The recovery of ASCs in cultures started with SLE patient BN cells was highly dependent on transient but early stimulation with anti-Ig.
source: Moreover, the recovery of ASCs in the cultures started with SLE patient BN cells was highly dependent on transient but early stimulation with anti-Ig as continuous stimulation with anti-Ig or no stimulation with anti-Ig reduced both the frequency and number of ASCs recovered in the cultures (Figure 8c–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 8c-d.

claim: Transient BCR stimulation was required for ASC development from SLE patient-derived BN cells activated with R848, IFNγ, IL-2 and IL-21.
source: Thus, these data indicated that transient BCR stimulation was required for ASC development from SLE patient-derived BN cells activated with R848, IFNγ, IL-2 and IL-21.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the experimental data with SLE patient cells.

claim: ASCs were easily identified in the day 2.5 cultures containing T-bethi DN2 cells.
source: Consistent with our predictions, ASCs were easily identified in the day 2.5 cultures containing T-bethi DN2 cells (Figure 8e).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISPOT data shown in Figure 8e.

claim: ASC recovery from T-bethi DN2 cells was at least 50-fold higher than BN cultures and only 2–3 times less than that seen with the memory B cell populations.
source: Indeed, ASC recovery was at least 50-fold higher in T-bethi DN2 cell cultures compared to the BN cultures and only 2–3 times less than that seen with the memory B cell populations (Figure 8e).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative ELISPOT data shown in Figure 8e.

claim: The expanded population of T-bethi DN2 cells present in some SLE patients likely represent a population of IFNγ, TLR ligand and antigen programmed primary effectors that can rapidly differentiate in a BCR-signaling independent manner into ASCs following IL-21 exposure.
source: These data therefore suggested that the expanded population of T-bethi DN2 cells present in some SLE patients likely represent a population of IFNγ, TLR ligand and antigen programmed primary effectors that can rapidly differentiate in a BCR-signaling independent manner into ASCs following IL-21 exposure.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the combined functional data with SLE patient DN2 cells.

claim: IFNγ promotes the in vitro formation of a T-bethiIRF4int IgDnegCD27neg (BDN) population that is similar to the T-bet expressing CD11chiCXCR5neg BDN (DN2 cells) subset found in SLE patients.
source: Here we show that IFNγ promotes the in vitro formation of a T-bethiIRF4int IgDnegCD27neg (BDN) population that is similar to the T-bet expressing CD11chiCXCR5neg BDN (referred to as DN2 cells) subset found in SLE patients (Jenks et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined experimental data and citation to Jenks et al., 2018.

claim: Both the in vitro generated T-bethiIRF4int BDN cells and SLE patient-derived DN2 cells exhibit transcriptional and functional properties of pre-ASCs.
source: Both the in vitro generated T-bethiIRF4int BDN cells and SLE patient-derived DN2 cells (Jenks et al., 2018) exhibit transcriptional and functional properties of pre-ASCs
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq and functional data comparing in vitro and patient-derived cells, with citation to Jenks et al., 2018.

claim: B cell intrinsic IFNγR signals could regulate human ASC responses.
source: suggesting that B cell intrinsic IFNγR signals could regulate human ASC responses.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: IFNγ signals enhance autoAb responses in mice.
source: While this hypothesis is supported by mouse experiments showing that IFNγ signals enhance autoAb responses (Domeier et al., 2016; Jackson et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Domeier et al., 2016; Jackson et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2012.

claim: B cell expression of the IFNγR and T-bet play a role in ASC development in mice.
source: and recent studies from our group demonstrating a role for B cell expression of the IFNγR and the IFNγ-inducible transcription factor T-bet in ASC development (Stone et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Stone et al., 2019.

claim: IFNγ has only very modest effects on activation and differentiation of human B cells.
source: In fact, prior data showing that IFNγ has only very modest effects on activation and differentiation of human B cells (Nakagawa et al., 1985; Splawski et al., 1989; Rousset et al., 1991)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nakagawa et al., 1985; Splawski et al., 1989; Rousset et al., 1991.

claim: Patients deficient in STAT1 produce Abs in response to some vaccines.
source: and that patients deficient in the IFN-activated transcription factor STAT1 produce Abs in response to some vaccines (Chapgier et al., 2009; Chapgier et al., 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chapgier et al., 2009; Chapgier et al., 2006.

claim: Human B cells can differentiate in the absence of IFNγ-induced signals.
source: Our in vitro studies do not contradict this conclusion as we also find that human B cells can differentiate in the absence of IFNγ-induced signals.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the experimental data showing ASC formation without IFNγ.

claim: B cell intrinsic IFNγ signals significantly enhance ASC differentiation induced in response to stimulation with anti-Ig, TLR7/8 ligand, IL-2 and IL-21.
source: However, we show that B cell intrinsic IFNγ signals significantly enhance ASC differentiation induced in response to stimulation with anti-Ig, TLR7/8 ligand, IL-2 and IL-21.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data showing enhanced ASC formation with IFNγ.

claim: 5- to 10 fold more ASCs are routinely recovered in BN cultures that contain IFNγ or IFNγ-producing T cells compared to cultures that lack IFNγ.
source: Indeed, we routinely recover 5- to 10 fold more ASCs in the BN cultures that contain IFNγ or IFNγ-producing T cells compared to cultures that lack IFNγ.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from multiple experiments.

claim: IFNγ signaling has the potential to augment ASC development in settings, like autoimmunity and viral infection, where IFNγ and TLR ligands are present.
source: Thus, we argue that IFNγ signaling has the potential to augment ASC development in settings, like autoimmunity and viral infection, where IFNγ and TLR ligands are present.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: IFNγ is not a B cell mitogen.
source: IFNγ is not, in and of itself, a B cell mitogen and is reported to induce apoptosis of human B cells (Bernabei et al., 2001; Sammicheli et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bernabei et al., 2001; Sammicheli et al., 2011.

claim: IFNγ synergizes with TLR7/8 ligand to promote multiple rounds of B cell proliferation.
source: However, we find that IFNγ synergizes with TLR7/8 ligand to promote multiple rounds of B cell proliferation – an important prerequisite of human ASC differentiation (Tangye et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by proliferation data and citation to Tangye et al., 2003.

claim: IFNγ and TLR7 signals cooperate to promote upregulation of Bcl6 and the acquisition of a germinal center-like phenotype in human B cells.
source: Although in vitro experiments using human B cells show that IFNγ can synergize with TLR7 and CD40 signals to promote upregulation of Bcl6 and the acquisition of a germinal center-like phenotype (Jackson et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jackson et al., 2016.

claim: IFNα-directed signals can enhance TLR7-mediated human B cell differentiation.
source: These results are analogous to studies showing that IFNα-directed signals can enhance TLR7-mediated human B cell differentiation (Jego et al., 2003; Bekeredjian-Ding et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jego et al., 2003; Bekeredjian-Ding et al., 2005.

claim: There is considerable overlap between genes regulated by IFNα and IFNγ.
source: Given the considerable overlap between genes regulated by IFNα and IFNγ (Pollard et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pollard et al., 2013.

claim: IFNα and IFNγ may augment TLR7 signaling in human B cells by similar mechanisms.
source: it is possible that IFNα and IFNγ may augment TLR7 signaling in human B cells by similar mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the overlap in IFNα and IFNγ regulated genes.

claim: IFNγ cooperates with IL-2, BCR, TLR7/8 ligand to globally alter the epigenetic landscape of the activated B cells.
source: First, we show that IFNγ cooperates with IL-2, BCR, TLR7/8 ligand to globally alter the epigenetic landscape of the activated B cells and to specifically increase chromatin accessibility surrounding NF-κB, STAT5 and T-bet binding sites.
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data showing global chromatin changes.

claim: IFNγ signaling induces increased T-bet expression and alterations in chromatin accessibility around T-bet binding sites.
source: While it is not particularly surprising that IFNγ signaling induces increased T-bet expression and alterations in chromatin accessibility around T-bet binding sites (see for example Iwata et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Iwata et al., 2017.

claim: IFNγ must augment TLR7/8 and IL-2-dependent signaling.
source: the finding that chromatin accessibility surrounding NF-κB and STAT5 binding motifs is also regulated by IFNγ suggests that IFNγ must augment TLR7/8 and IL-2-dependent signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the ATAC-seq data showing increased accessibility at NF-κB and STAT5 sites.

claim: IFNγ promotes commitment to the ASC lineage by inducing expression of IRF4 and modifying chromatin accessibility surrounding IRF4-binding sites.
source: Second, we show that IFNγ promotes commitment to the ASC lineage by inducing expression of IRF4 and modifying chromatin accessibility surrounding IRF4-binding sites within regulatory regions in the genome of the activated BN cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry and ATAC-seq data showing IRF4 expression and accessibility changes.

claim: IFNγ signals promote chromatin accessibility within the PRDM1 (BLIMP1) locus.
source: Third, we find that IFNγ signals promote chromatin accessibility within the PRDM1 (BLIMP1) locus and initiate chromatin remodeling around BLIMP1-binding sites within the genome of the activated BN cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data showing DARs at the PRDM1 locus.

claim: IFNγ signals alter chromatin accessibility within the IL21R locus of the activated BN cells.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that IFNγ signals alter chromatin accessibility within the IL21R locus of the activated BN cells and that this change in accessibility is associated with IFNγ-dependent, increased expression of the IL-21R by the activated BN cells and with increased responsiveness of these cells to IL-21, as measured by phosphorylation of STAT3.
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data showing DARs at the IL21R locus.

claim: IFNγ signals, when combined with BCR, TLR and IL-2R signals, poise human BN cells to differentiate in response to IL-21.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that IFNγ signals, when combined with BCR, TLR and IL-2R signals, poise human BN cells to differentiate in response to IL-21.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the combined epigenetic and functional data.

claim: SNPs in the human TLR7 locus are associated with increased SLE susceptibility.
source: Signaling through TLR7 is known to be important in SLE as prior studies reveal that SNPs in the human TLR7 locus (Lee et al., 2016) and overexpression of TLR7 in mice (Pisitkun et al., 2006) are associated with increased SLE susceptibility
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2016; Pisitkun et al., 2006.

claim: Overexpression of TLR7 in mice is associated with increased SLE susceptibility.
source: Signaling through TLR7 is known to be important in SLE as prior studies reveal that SNPs in the human TLR7 locus (Lee et al., 2016) and overexpression of TLR7 in mice (Pisitkun et al., 2006) are associated with increased SLE susceptibility
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pisitkun et al., 2006.

claim: Deletion of TLR7 protects mice from the development of SLE.
source: while deletion of TLR7 protects mice from the development of SLE (Christensen et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Christensen et al., 2006.

claim: Deletion of T-bet in B lineage cells prevents autoAb responses in a mouse model of TLR7-dependent SLE.
source: Our data show that deletion of the IFNγ-inducible transcription factor T-bet in B lineage cells prevents autoAb responses in a mouse model (Pisitkun et al., 2006) of TLR7-dependent SLE.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the mouse bone marrow chimera experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citation to Pisitkun et al., 2006.

claim: B cell intrinsic IFNγ signaling induces a TLR7/8 hyperresponsive state in human B cells.
source: Moreover, our data demonstrates that B cell intrinsic IFNγ signaling induces a TLR7/8 hyperresponsive state in human B cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing synergy between IFNγ and low-dose R848.

claim: IFNγ-exposed BN cells can respond and differentiate into ASCs when exposed to 100-fold lower concentration of TLR7/8 ligands than normally used to activate B cells.
source: Rather, we find that IFNγ-exposed BN cells can respond and differentiate into ASCs when exposed to 100-fold lower concentration of TLR7/8 ligands than normally used to activate B cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 6.

claim: B cells from autoimmune patients with detectable systemic levels IFNγ will be highly sensitive to the presence of endogenous and exogenously derived TLR7 ligands.
source: Given that we observed that even low levels of IFNγ are sufficient to synergize with suboptimal concentrations of TLR7/8 ligands, we predict that B cells from autoimmune patients with detectable systemic levels IFNγ will be highly sensitive to the presence of endogenous and exogenously derived TLR7 ligands.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the in vitro data.

claim: TLR7-driven ASC responses are likely to be further enhanced in individuals who have increased levels of circulating IFNγ.
source: Our data predict that TLR7-driven ASC responses are likely to be further enhanced in individuals who have increased levels of circulating IFNγ.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: SLE patients who have higher systemic levels of IFNγ also have more T-bethi DN2 cells and higher autoAb titers.
source: Consistent with this, we show that SLE patients who have higher systemic levels of IFNγ also have more T-bethi DN2 cells and higher autoAb titers.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The size of the T-bethi DN2 population correlates with disease activity, particularly in African-American SLE patients.
source: We and others (Wang et al., 2018; Jenks et al., 2018) also report that the size of the T-bethi DN2 population correlates with disease activity, particularly in African-American SLE patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2018; Jenks et al., 2018.

claim: T-bethi DN2 cells are unlikely to represent a purely 'pathogenic' population.
source: However, it is important to note that T-bethi DN2 cells are unlikely to represent a purely 'pathogenic' population
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation of vaccine-specific T-bethi cells in healthy individuals.

claim: An inducible population of vaccine-specific T-bethi CD27neg DN2 cells is found in healthy individuals who were immunized with inactivated influenza virus.
source: as we also find an inducible population of vaccine-specific T-bethi CD27neg DN2 cells in healthy individuals who were immunized with inactivated influenza virus (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by unpublished data mentioned in the text.

claim: A T-bet expressing CD27+CD21lo switched memory subset with pre-ASC attributes is induced following vaccination or infection.
source: Similarly, others report (Lau et al., 2017; Knox et al., 2017) a T-bet expressing CD27+CD21lo switched memory subset with pre-ASC attributes, which is induced following vaccination or infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lau et al., 2017; Knox et al., 2017.

claim: T-bethi B cells found in HD and autoimmune patients in the settings of acute and chronic inflammation are formed in an IFNγ-dependent manner.
source: Thus, we speculate that the T-bethi B cells, which are found in HD and autoimmune patients in the settings of acute and chronic inflammation driven by vaccination, infection, autoimmunity and aging, are formed in an IFNγ-dependent manner
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the combined data.

claim: T-bethi B cells likely represent a pool of primary and secondary pre-ASCs as well as effector memory B cells that are epigenetically poised to differentiate.
source: and likely represent a pool of primary and secondary pre-ASCs as well as effector memory B cells that are epigenetically poised to differentiate.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the functional and epigenetic data.

claim: The DN2 cells likely arise in an IFNγ-dependent fashion in SLE patients.
source: Since the expansion of the T-bethi DN2 cells in SLE patients correlates with systemic levels of IFNγ and IFNγ-induced cytokines, we postulate that the DN2 cells likely arise in an IFNγ-dependent fashion in these patients.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the correlation data.

claim: The IFNγ-directed changes in chromatin accessibility within the IL21R and PRDM1 loci seen in the in vitro generated T-bethiIRF4int pre-ASCs are also found in T-bethi DN2 cells isolated from SLE patients.
source: In support of this possibility, we demonstrate that the IFNγ-directed changes in chromatin accessibility within the IL21R and PRDM1 loci seen in the in vitro generated T-bethiIRF4int pre-ASCs are also found in T-bethi DN2 cells isolated from SLE patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data comparison shown in Figure 7j-k.

claim: The molecular properties of the SLE DN2 subset and the in vitro generated IFNγ-dependent T-bethi BDN cells are similar and unique when compared to conventional memory B cells or BN cells.
source: Moreover, we show that the molecular properties of the SLE DN2 subset and the in vitro generated IFNγ-dependent T-bethi BDN cells are similar and unique when compared to conventional memory B cells or BN cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the combined transcriptional and functional data.

claim: IFNγ primes the T-bethi BDN cells to respond to subthreshold concentrations of R848.
source: For example, as discussed above, IFNγ primes the T-bethi BDN cells to respond to subthreshold concentrations of R848.
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data.

claim: SLE DN2 cells make augmented responses to TLR7/8-stimulation compared to other B cell subsets.
source: Similarly, SLE DN2 cells make augmented responses to TLR7/8-stimulation compared to other B cell subsets (Jenks et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jenks et al., 2018.

claim: SLE patient DN2 pre-ASCs and the in vitro generated T-bethi BDN subset can differentiate without a need for additional BCR stimulation.
source: We also show that SLE patient DN2 pre-ASCs and the in vitro generated T-bethi BDN subset can differentiate without a need for additional BCR stimulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by functional data shown in Figures 3 and 8.

claim: Both the SLE DN2 subset and the in vitro generated T-bethi BDN subset require IL-21 to differentiate into ASCs.
source: However, like BN cells (Deenick et al., 2013), both the SLE DN2 subset (Wang et al., 2018; Jenks et al., 2018) and the in vitro generated T-bethi BDN subset require IL-21 to differentiate into ASCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Deenick et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2018; Jenks et al., 2018 and experimental data.

claim: The in vitro pre-ASC cultures could be used to better understand the development, maintenance and functional attributes of the T-bethi DN2 cells that are expanded and associated with more severe disease in SLE patients.

claim: A phase I trial examining IFNγ blockade in SLE patients did not reveal a therapeutic benefit.

claim: T-bethi DN2 cells are most expanded in African American patients with severe disease.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2018; Jenks et al., 2018.

claim: Future studies evaluating the efficacy of IFNγ blockade in SLE patients should focus specifically on the subset of patients who present with elevated IFNγ levels and significant expansion of the IFNγ-inducible T-bet expressing DN2 pre-ASC population.
source: we propose that future studies evaluating the efficacy of IFNγ blockade in SLE patients should focus specifically on the subset of patients who present with elevated IFNγ levels and significant expansion of the IFNγ-inducible T-bet expressing DN2 pre-ASC population.
evidence: The claim is speculative, representing a proposal for future research based on the current findings.
